I am fifty-nine this year, and I have farmed these fields in Quzhou for over three decades. Having gone to university back when few village boys did, I learned to read the soil and the markets with more patience than most of my neighbors. My body is not what it was, so I plan my labor carefully and rely on good seed and sound management rather than brute work.

It is early spring now. My winter wheat, sown last October, is greening up on ten mu. I chose **Luyuan 502** — an improved variety with good resistance and stable yield — and I will manage it carefully: a rotary tillage before sowing gave me a fine seedbed, and now I will top-dress with nitrogen and irrigate three more times before June harvest. I expect about 1,050 jin per mu. Wheat is my foundation; it feeds my family and the market price is reliable.

After the wheat comes off in early June, I will immediately plant **Denghai 605** hybrid maize on the same ten mu. I use no-tillage for maize — I have done this for years. The soil structure stays intact, I save fuel and labor, and with the wheat stubble returned to the field, the moisture holds better. Two irrigations and two pesticide sprays are enough for a good summer maize crop; I expect around 1,150 jin per mu.

On the remaining two mu, I am planting **Guoxinmian** cotton in April. Cotton is labor-intensive — it needs about ten pesticide applications and careful watering — but the income per mu is higher than grain, and two mu is a size I can manage without hiring too much help. I rotary-till the cotton plot and apply a balanced fertilizer with more phosphorus and potassium to support boll development. I expect roughly 550 jin of seed cotton per mu.

My university education taught me one thing above all: do not waste inputs. I apply fertilizer by growth stage, I water when the crop needs it rather than by habit, and I rotate my chemicals to avoid resistance. At my age, I have seen good years and bad, but this steady plan — wheat for security, maize for volume, cotton for cash — is what I trust.
